articles.title: The Nvidia Scandal and the China Business Problem We Keep Seeing
articles.content:
Around twenty years ago, an American company called us because its $2 million order of Christmas tree lights was not going to arrive in the United States until December. For a company selling Christmas lights, December delivery is a disaster. We contacted the Chinese factory, only to learn that the people there had never heard of our client. After speaking with the factory and reviewing Chinese-language documents, we discovered that the American company had unknowingly been dealing through a sourcing agent that owed money to the factory. The factory had stopped production because it had not been paid, and our client had no direct contract with the company actually making its products. The American buyer ended up paying millions more to get its lights delivered in time.
I have told that story for years because the underlying mistake is so common. A company thinks it knows its Chinese manufacturer because it has been doing business with the same people for years. It knows who sends the invoices, who answers the emails, and where to wire the money. What it sometimes doesn't know is which company actually controls production, who owns the assets, and who will be responsible when something goes wrong. As I explain in our guide to overseas manufacturing due diligence, those are things you need to establish before sending money or committing your business to a supplier. The scandal surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO, Jensen Huang, has brought a much larger and more complicated version of these questions into public view.
On November 12, 2026, Nvidia announced Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO amid revelations of his affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese businesswoman and former executive of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based purchaser of Nvidia's advanced computing equipment. American intelligence officials reportedly suspect Alice Huang of having connections to Chinese intelligence. China denies those allegations, and no public proceeding has established that she engaged in espionage or that Jensen Huang was coerced into acting on China's behalf. Much of the coverage has focused on the affair and its national security implications, but the business relationships surrounding Megaspeed deserve attention too. According to The Washington Post's investigation, Megaspeed's assets increased from approximately $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024. A relatively obscure company had become a major purchaser of some of America's most strategically sensitive technology, yet basic questions remained about who financed and controlled it and where its chips ultimately went.
My longtime friend David Dayton recently wrote an excellent article about the controversy, I Don't Own a Leather Jacket or Have a Chinese Mistress. David has spent more than 30 years working in China and Southeast Asia, speaks Mandarin and Thai, and understands Chinese business as well as anyone I know. His article examines the leverage China's business and political system gives the government over companies and individuals. I share many of his concerns, particularly those involving opaque business relationships and the financial pressures facing Chinese manufacturers. Our law firm regularly encounters both problems, usually without the billion-dollar transactions or espionage allegations.
David also points readers to an analysis by Desmond Shum, whose book Red Roulette described the complicated relationships among businesspeople, political figures, and wealth in China. In Alice Huang: The Spy Narrative Misses Her Real Business, Shum suggests Alice Huang may have been operating as a commercial intermediary, or what Chinese businesspeople sometimes call a white glove. A white glove acts on behalf of others while obscuring the identity or interests of the people behind a transaction. Shum traces Huang's involvement in Chinese investment firms, offshore holding companies, and corporate acquisitions. His theory is that her value may have come from arranging transactions and financing for business interests whose involvement was not readily apparent. I find his analysis plausible, though it remains a theory.
Government investigations have since added important facts. On November 12, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs disclosed that its police and customs authorities had begun investigating Megaspeed and related parties in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving computer servers. Singapore questioned Alice Huang in June 2025 and held her passport while investigating. In February 2026, it concluded there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed the suspected declaration-related offenses. It also determined that she had knowingly provided investigators inaccurate information to minimize her role in Megaspeed. Singapore issued her a stern warning, barred her from returning, and expressly stated that it had not investigated her for espionage.
A subsequent joint statement from the U.S. Departments of Commerce and Justice disclosed that Commerce began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 over possible semiconductor diversion. In May 2025, investigators requested Nvidia's records concerning sales to Megaspeed. The following month, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list, and American officials conducted an on-site end-use check in Singapore. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in a criminal investigation. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and has retained outside counsel to investigate the allegations concerning its business, and neither government has established that it unlawfully diverted Nvidia chips.
The United States has also tightened its export controls. A Commerce Department rule effective November 19, 2026 addresses certain advanced semiconductor transactions and arrangements through which companies in restricted jurisdictions obtain significant computing capacity from overseas data centers. For covered transactions, the rule calls for due diligence concerning direct and indirect ownership or control by persons in specified restricted jurisdictions.
According to The Wire China's investigation, Alice Huang served as Megaspeed's managing director from March to November 2023, when the company's shares were transferred to another Singapore entity, Swiftdata. Yet Singapore identified her as Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson, and a key controller during its 2025 investigation, American officials interviewed her as CEO in June 2025, and Megaspeed itself says she did not leave the company until August 2025. Those records were not necessarily misleading, because someone can give up a registered directorship and keep running a business. That is exactly why a company's registered owners and directors do not always tell you who is making its decisions.
Most foreign companies doing business in China will never encounter anything resembling the Megaspeed investigation. Their problems are far more ordinary. They purchase products, pay deposits, provide technical information, and expect their suppliers to perform. Trouble begins when the company named in the contract is not the company controlling what matters.
My colleague Arlo Kipfer recently wrote about a U.S. company our firm represented that had been buying molded plastic products from what it believed was a single Guangdong manufacturing operation. For nearly two years, everything ran through a Hong Kong company that provided quotations, issued invoices, accepted payments, and described the mainland factory as its own production facility. Then the American buyer found a less expensive supplier and decided to move production. When it asked for its molds back, the Hong Kong company explained that it did not own the factory and had no molds to return. The mainland factory was a separate legal entity with which our client had never contracted, and it claimed ownership of the molds because it had paid the toolmaker to produce them.
Our client had spent substantial money on tooling it could not establish that it owned. The factory holding the molds had signed no agreement with our client, while the Hong Kong company that signed the contract had no control over the molds. That is an especially bad position to be in after deciding to change manufacturers. Hong Kong intermediaries can perform perfectly legitimate and valuable functions, including sales, financing, logistics, and export documentation. But related companies remain legally distinct unless there is a basis for holding one responsible for another's obligations. You cannot assume that a mainland factory is bound by a contract merely because the Hong Kong intermediary calls it "our factory." Depending on the transaction, proper protection may require a direct agreement with the factory, a three-party contract, a guarantee, or separate agreements allocating responsibilities among the companies involved.
Our lawyers frequently encounter international manufacturing disputes where the company that signed the agreement has few assets and the company holding the products, molds, or technical information never agreed to return them. Sometimes the legal claims are strong enough to pursue. Other times we have to tell the client that litigation would probably cost more than it could realistically recover. That is a terrible conversation to have with a business owner who believed a signed contract meant the company was protected.
A manufacturer that controls the assets your business needs can have enormous leverage even when your contracts identify the correct company. A recent example involved an American company whose Chinese factory demanded an immediate 34% price increase. The factory held the company's molds and designs and had access to its customer information. Two years earlier, the buyer had signed a single agreement that mixed manufacturing, NNN, and tooling provisions together. When our lawyers reviewed it, they found overlapping provisions and unclear remedies. We advised against suing to recover the molds because the contract was too muddled and obtaining useful relief was too uncertain. We recommended making replacement molds as quickly as possible. Unfortunately, the new molds took longer than expected, and the resulting production shutdown nearly bankrupted the company. I discuss that matter in China Manufacturing Contracts: When One Agreement Is Not Enough.
The factory's power came from its possession of assets the buyer needed to keep operating. Even if the customer believed it had a valid legal claim, it could not afford to wait months for a resolution while its business was falling apart. I have seen companies spend a great deal of time negotiating contractual protections that look impressive on paper while giving surprisingly little attention to whether they can actually enforce those protections against a manufacturer that refuses to cooperate.
Another client came to us after telling its Chinese manufacturer it wanted to add a second factory to accommodate increased demand. The manufacturer responded by claiming ownership of the Chinese trademarks and patents covering our client's products. It threatened to seek injunctions against any other Chinese factory that attempted to manufacture or export those products. Six lawsuits later, the parties reached a settlement. What troubles me most about that case is that the American company had not threatened to leave China or reduce its orders. It simply wanted more manufacturing capacity. I wrote about that dispute in How to Negotiate Lower China Manufacturing Prices Without Putting Your Business at Risk.
Some Chinese manufacturers respond constructively when a buyer asks for lower prices or additional production capacity. Others react aggressively to requests the buyer considers entirely reasonable. Sometimes the factory has a legitimate contractual position. Sometimes it is using whatever legal or practical leverage it possesses to protect its business, including claims that ultimately prove difficult to sustain. Before advising a client to negotiate aggressively with an existing manufacturer, I want to know what that factory controls, what rights it can credibly assert, and how much damage it can cause if negotiations go badly. A company that thinks it is strengthening its bargaining position by threatening to move production may instead be warning its supplier to secure whatever leverage it has left.

Foreign customers often have little idea how serious those financial problems have become until their manufacturer starts demanding larger deposits, delaying shipments, substituting inferior materials, or refusing to release finished goods.
Not long ago, a Midwest furniture company wired $800,000 to a Chinese manufacturer it had worked with for nearly twenty years. The furniture never arrived. The factory closed, its owner disappeared, and the company was left with little realistic prospect of recovering its money. I described that case in China Manufacturing Risks: When Your Reliable Supplier Stops Being Reliable. That client had not selected an unknown factory based on an attractive website or a suspiciously low quotation. It had been doing business with the same manufacturer for almost two decades. The length of the relationship made the company comfortable, but it did nothing to protect the buyer when the factory failed.

If you depend on Chinese suppliers, compare the companies named in your contracts with the companies that actually receive your money, manufacture your products, hold your tooling, and possess your technical information. If they don't match, find out why. You may have a perfectly legitimate arrangement that needs better documentation, or you may discover that the company holding something essential to your business has never agreed to give it back.

During the worst of the U.S.-China tariff battles, companies regularly came to us after trying to find manufacturers in Mexico, Vietnam, or elsewhere. They had concluded that the alternatives could not make their products, could not make them at the required quality or volume, or were too expensive even after accounting for the China tariffs. We hear that story much less now. Most companies contacting us about manufacturing in China have already decided to manufacture there.
He then asked about China Plus One, or China+1, the practice of adding manufacturing or sourcing outside China to reduce dependence on it. I told him we still discuss it about once a month, usually because I raise it. Often the client is already in a dispute with a Chinese manufacturer or with Sinosure, China's state-owned export credit insurer. At that point I want to know what happens to the company's business if its Chinese factory stops shipping. The answer may matter more than the legal merits of the dispute.

China's advantage is the industrial system it has spent decades building. In one manufacturing region, a buyer can often find a capable factory, the component suppliers that feed it, the engineers who can fix a design problem, and the tooling shops that can make a replacement part in days. For a complicated product, having all of those people close together saves time and money that may never show up in a factory's quoted unit price.
This is especially important for small and midsize American importers, whose Chinese manufacturers may handle product development, component sourcing, tooling, packaging, and production. In another country the buyer may have to provide complete engineering files, arrange component supply, and manage far more of the process itself. A factory in Mexico or Vietnam might make an excellent product once the buyer solves those problems, but the cost of getting there can still make the move uneconomic. We have seen businesses spend months exploring alternatives and then decide to keep buying from China. I have no quarrel with that decision. The danger lies in assuming that a good relationship with one factory makes contingency planning unnecessary.
Consider a client we wrote about earlier this year. Its Chinese manufacturer demanded an immediate 34 percent price increase, and the factory had the client's molds, designs, and customer information. The buyer had signed a single agreement combining its manufacturing, tooling, and confidentiality protections, but the overlapping provisions and unclear remedies left it in a weak position. We advised against suing to recover the molds because, under that contract and in those circumstances, making new molds was likely to be quicker and less expensive. The new molds took longer than expected, production stopped, and the interruption nearly bankrupted the company.
Another American company told its Chinese manufacturer it needed a second factory to meet increased demand. It was not planning to leave China or even cut its purchases from the existing supplier. The factory nevertheless claimed ownership of the Chinese trademarks and patents covering the products and threatened to stop any other Chinese factory from making or exporting them. The parties settled, but only after six lawsuits in four different cities and two countries.
Those cases are why I ask about the buyer's ability to move production before discussing litigation strategy. I want to know who owns the molds, whether the buyer can actually retrieve them, and whether it has the native design files and specifications. I also want to know whether another factory could make the product and whether an unidentified subcontractor or component supplier has something the buyer cannot readily replace. A favorable judgment several years from now will not fill next month's customer orders.
Sinosure can make the calculation harder. A buyer that withholds payment over defective goods may find itself facing collection demands from Sinosure or its agents, and the dispute can affect its access to credit from other Chinese suppliers. We have handled more than 100 Sinosure matters, and one of my first questions is how much the company needs to keep sourcing from China. A business with no realistic alternative may need to approach the dispute differently from one that can keep operating elsewhere. Leaving China does not erase a legitimate debt or settle a contract claim, but it can change how dependent the buyer is on the Chinese manufacturing system while the claim is resolved.
A recent AmCham Shanghai article on China Plus One in Thailand features Mark Plum and Alex Bryant of East West Associates, who have spent decades helping companies manufacture in China and Southeast Asia. One of their clients wants to replicate its Suzhou production at a new facility in Rayong, Thailand, making the same product to the same standard in either location and shifting work between them as costs, freight, duties, demand, and capacity change. Thailand has a substantial manufacturing base in electronics, automotive components, appliances, and HVAC equipment, and its Board of Investment can offer valuable incentives for qualifying projects. A disruption involving Taiwan could affect shipping and manufacturing well beyond the Taiwan Strait, and China has used export controls on critical materials, including rare earths, in its trade disputes. On November 9, 2026, China's Ministry of Commerce extended the suspension of certain October 2025 export controls through January 10, 2027. If both of your factories need a critical material that only China can reliably supply, moving final assembly has not solved that risk.
U.S. tariff rules have changed repeatedly in 2026. On February 20, the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, Inc. v. That decision did not eliminate the longstanding China-specific Section 301 duties or tariffs imposed under other statutes. In July, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative imposed new Section 301 duties on imports from 60 economies over their failure to prohibit or effectively restrict imports made with forced labor.
China itself faces a new 12.5 percent duty on covered products, generally on top of its existing Section 301 tariffs. Vietnam and Thailand also face the new 12.5 percent duty on covered products, while Mexico faces 10 percent, with an exemption for goods entered duty-free under the USMCA. No universal percentage of local content automatically makes every product Thai, Vietnamese, or Mexican. Mexico is more complicated still because a product may have Mexican origin for one customs purpose and fail to qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA. As we explain in our guide to moving manufacturing from China to Mexico, the USMCA has product-specific requirements, and Chinese inputs can affect whether the finished product qualifies for preferential treatment when it enters the United States. At the July 1, 2026 joint review, the United States declined to renew the USMCA in its existing form, though the agreement remains in force.
The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act creates another risk for products manufactured outside China when they incorporate covered inputs from Xinjiang or from entities on the UFLPA Entity List. A company considering China+1 should review its existing Chinese manufacturing relationship before giving anyone else its designs or telling its current factory it might lose business. Verify who owns the tooling, whether the contract requires its return, who has the native CAD and other technical files, and whether your factory can legally withhold them. Register and protect important trademarks and other intellectual property in the countries where you manufacture and plan to manufacture. Our articles on China exit planning and IP and protecting IP when manufacturing beyond China explain why this work should come before the supplier learns of your plans.
We have seen what happens when a company gets the timing wrong. In one case we described years ago, a U.S. buyer told its Chinese manufacturer it would be moving production to Mexico and Thailand and then discovered that someone in China had registered its brand names and logos as trademarks in those countries. The company now faced an obstacle to manufacturing under its own brand in the very places it hoped to go. I would rather spend money on trademark searches and filings before the move than on a fight over who has the right to use the brand afterward.
Good contracts also matter when things go wrong. One client's Chinese manufacturing agreement clearly gave it ownership of the molds at its factory. When the factory refused to release them, we retained Chinese litigation counsel, filed suit, and secured a court order freezing the manufacturer's bank accounts within about five days. The factory released the molds the next day. We have written about that case and why the contract mattered. The result was unusually quick, and the availability of that remedy depends on the facts and the local court. It is a useful contrast with the company forced to remake its molds after its contract failed to give it a practical path to recovery.
Once a new manufacturer is identified, the legal work continues. The agreement needs to fit the country's law and the actual production arrangement. The buyer needs clear rights over its designs, tooling, and product-development work, enforceable specifications and quality standards, meaningful restrictions on unauthorized subcontracting, and a sensible way to resolve disputes against the party that actually controls production. A Chinese NNN or manufacturing agreement should not simply be relabeled for use in Thailand or Vietnam. A company building its own factory, rather than hiring a contract manufacturer, also has investment, labor, tax, and environmental requirements to deal with.
Start with the product, not a list of supposedly hot manufacturing countries. Thailand may be an excellent choice for an electronics or appliance maker and Mexico for products sold mainly in North America, but what matters is whether an actual factory can meet your specifications, volume, price, delivery needs, and compliance requirements, using components it can reliably obtain. Count the complete landed cost of the finished product and the expense of managing a second supplier. I see no point in moving production if it means worse products or costs that make your business uncompetitive.
For many smaller businesses, I would begin by qualifying a backup manufacturer without immediately moving a large portion of production. Have it make samples and, where feasible, a trial production run. Verify its legal identity and capabilities, see whether its suppliers can support the product, and establish how long it would take to increase production if the Chinese factory stopped. At the same time, secure the rights and technical information you need to use that backup. Some companies will find that meaningful diversification is too expensive for now. They will at least know their exposure and can decide whether additional inventory, alternative components, or better contracts would reduce it.
I am happy to help a client keep manufacturing in China when China remains its best option. What I do not want is for that client to discover, in the middle of a fight over invoices or molds, that nobody else can make its product and that its current factory knows it.

articles.title: How to Negotiate Lower China Manufacturing Prices
articles.content:
A U.S. company came to us after telling its Chinese manufacturer that it needed a second factory to handle increased production. The manufacturer responded by claiming it owned the Chinese trademarks and patents covering the company's products. It threatened to seek injunctions against any other Chinese factory that tried to make those products or export them from China. Six lawsuits later, the parties reached a settlement. The company hadn't threatened to leave China or reduce its purchases. It simply needed more manufacturing capacity.
I've seen Chinese factories agree to large price reductions, sometimes with surprisingly little resistance. I've also seen companies get themselves into serious trouble by making what they considered reasonable requests for lower prices. A manufacturer that believes its customer is preparing to leave may claim ownership of molds and intellectual property, resurrect old debts, or threaten to stop production. All of these have happened, and the resulting problems can cost far more than the hoped-for savings. I favor negotiating lower manufacturing prices when the circumstances justify it, but before approaching your Chinese factory, you should know what leverage each side has and what might happen if negotiations go badly.
Yes. Our international manufacturing lawyers have coached clients into getting reductions of 25 percent or more, and a few have achieved reductions as large as 50 percent. Some negotiated those savings by increasing purchase volumes or extending their manufacturing relationships. Others obtained double-digit reductions without making additional commitments. These are actual results, but I wouldn't tell every company to expect anything close to them. YMMV.
For years, Chinese manufacturers faced intense price competition, weak demand in certain industries, and pressure from foreign buyers moving production elsewhere. In February 2024, Reuters published China's Tumbling Prices Push Some Exporters to the Brink. It described a Chinese lighting manufacturer that accepted a $1.5 million order at a price 25 percent below what it had charged for a similar order the previous year. Worse, the new price was 10 percent below production cost. The manufacturer was willing to lose money rather than risk losing the customer and potentially shutting down production. For decades, people talked about "The China Price" to describe China's extraordinarily low manufacturing costs. I started calling situations like the one Reuters described as the China Desperation Price.
China's manufacturing economy has since changed. According to China's National Bureau of Statistics, producer prices rose 5 percent year over year in September 2026, while factories' input costs rose nearly 7 percent. Prices were still falling in some industries, including automobile manufacturing. Rising costs can make price cuts harder to get, but national statistics tell you little about what your own factory will charge. What we're seeing is that major manufacturers like Midea and Foxconn are thriving, while many smaller, less specialized factories are struggling. If you're a small company asking Midea for a price reduction, you have far less bargaining power than a company that buys 55 percent of a small factory's total annual production.
You also need to know why a factory is offering a reduction and whether it can afford the new price. A manufacturer with idle capacity might accept a smaller margin to keep its workers busy. Some factories agree to attractive prices and then substitute cheaper materials, delay production, or demand additional payments. A 20 percent price reduction won't help much if you end up with defective products or miss a major delivery deadline.
Tariffs have given American companies another reason to seek lower prices from Chinese manufacturers. When President Trump imposed heavy tariffs on Chinese products during his first administration, many American buyers asked their suppliers to absorb some of the additional expense. The same issue has arisen as U.S.-China tariff policies have continued changing. I've seen this approach work, particularly when the factory values the relationship and understands that higher import costs threaten future orders. Some manufacturers prefer a smaller margin to losing a good customer.
Before using tariffs to justify a price reduction, make sure you know which duties actually apply to your products. Product classification, country of origin, trade measures, and exclusions all affect what an American importer owes. The U.S. International Trade Commission's Harmonized Tariff Schedule is a good starting point, but you also need to understand your total landed costs, including freight, insurance, tariffs, and other import expenses. Tariff reduction is not a one-hour fix, and lowering import costs often involves more than getting your factory to cut its prices. I would much rather see a company use tariffs to explain why it needs lower prices than threaten to move production to Mexico. That threat might work, but it can also convince your factory you're already planning to leave. Don't make that threat unless you're prepared to leave, because your factory may treat you as if you already have.
Chinese manufacturers sometimes interpret a request for lower prices as a warning that their customer is looking for another supplier. I've written about the resulting problems in Leaving China Manufacturing: The Hidden Risks and How to Protect Your Business.
One company paid $80,000 for five molds used across three product lines. Eight months later, when the company needed those molds, its Chinese manufacturer refused to release them without additional payment. The client eventually paid $200,000 to recover property it had already purchased. The dispute also shut down production for two months, costing approximately $800,000 in lost revenue. The buyer needed its molds, had customers waiting, and had no alternative manufacturer ready to take over, so the factory held all the leverage. Variations of this problem are common. Manufacturers claim tooling was never fully paid for or demand additional compensation for development work, and some simply refuse to release it. Buyers then discover their contracts provide little protection against losing access to equipment essential to their production. The time to address tooling ownership and recovery is while your relationship with the factory is still good, and before you start negotiating for lower pricing.
A U.S. company told its Chinese manufacturer that it might move production to Mexico or Thailand if the factory refused to lower its prices. The company later discovered that someone in China had registered its brand names and logos as trademarks in both Mexico and Thailand. Its ability to manufacture products under its own brands in those countries was now threatened. Similar problems arise inside China. Foreign buyers discover that someone else has registered trademarks or patents covering their products, and sometimes that someone is the manufacturer. Those registrations can be used to threaten replacement manufacturers, interfere with production, or seek the detention of products at Chinese ports. The six-lawsuit case at the beginning of this article involved a factory claiming IP rights that could prevent its customer from using another Chinese manufacturer.
In another case, an American company discovered that its Chinese manufacturer had registered 17 of its trademarks without permission. The manufacturer then approached the American company's two giant retail customers, offering the same products at prices 40 percent lower. Foreign companies still want Chinese customers, but many have lost their appetite for putting employees and substantial assets in China. A U.S. furniture manufacturer we represent wanted its American employees out of China, and it ended up selling its China business to the manager who ran it and financing most of the sale. I have favored using Chinese distributors for years, and I have watched Western companies spend a fortune trying to sell good products in China on their own, with disappointing results.
Selling in China is hard, and most of the clichés about doing business there have some truth to them. It is not one market, and you can do well in Shanghai and get nowhere in another city. A capable Chinese distributor knows the customers and has people on the ground to deal with the messiness of selling there, but the wrong one can tie up your market for years while selling almost nothing.
A distributor takes on much of the sales work and, depending on the agreement, after-sales support. The foreign supplier avoids the cost of a Chinese subsidiary and its employment, tax, and administrative obligations. Some of our clients have well-known products in China and no office or employees there. For other ways to reach Chinese customers without setting up a local company, see 6 Smart Strategies for Selling to China Without Being in China.
Using a distributor does not end the foreign supplier's China obligations. It still has to comply with Chinese product rules and protect its trademarks, and collecting from the distributor is its problem too. For many of our clients, the smaller physical presence is still worth a great deal, and keeping employees out of China also lowers the risk of exit bans arising from commercial disputes.
I start out skeptical of a distributor that approaches you first, because wanting your product says nothing about whether it can sell it. I want to know what a prospective distributor has actually sold, where it has sold it, and who buys from it. "National coverage" often turns out to mean a warehouse and two salespeople, so a company claiming a nationwide network ought to be able to name its salespeople and the customers they cover. Check its ownership and litigation history, and look hard at its finances, including whether it has the money to promote a new product or expects you to pay for the entire launch.
Experience with other foreign suppliers is useful, especially when those relationships have lasted. Ask for references and actually call them. Then ask my favorite question: How does our product fit with what you already sell? A distributor with complementary products can be an excellent choice. If it is making good money selling competing products, look much harder. Good China due diligence catches some of these problems before anyone signs.
Clients often bring us distribution agreements that have worked in Europe, the United States, or Australia. We use them as a starting point because they reflect how the client does business, but we almost always rewrite substantial parts of them for China, and the issues below are where most of that rewriting happens. We cover the questions we ask before drafting in China Distribution Contracts: The Questions We Ask.
The first question is who sells to the Chinese customer. A conventional distributor buys from the foreign supplier and resells on its own account. An agent finds customers and helps arrange sales for the supplier, usually for a commission. Our clients generally prefer the distributor model because the Chinese company takes direct responsibility for local sales and customer payments, and because it makes clear who handles importation.
Chinese law looks beyond what the contract calls the distributor to how the relationship actually works. A distributor that routinely signs contracts on your behalf can create Chinese tax exposure for you. Depending on the structure, the arrangement can also fall under China's franchise rules, which turn on how the business operates, including the rights the foreign supplier grants and the fees it collects.
I pay close attention to titles and authority. A distributor's key person often needs a serious title, such as China Director, to get meetings, above all with government buyers. We pair that title with a board-approved authorization letter that spells out exactly what the person can and cannot do on the client's behalf, for reasons we explain in Setting Up Your Chinese Distributor for Success: Titles and Authority Matter. The agreement needs to say whether the distributor can use sub-distributors and who answers for their conduct. Anti-bribery provisions belong here too. They matter most when the customers include state-owned enterprises or government bodies, and they need to address both Chinese law and, where it applies, the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.
I have lost count of how many problems began with a foreign company assuming that its U.S. or European trademark registration protected it in China. China is primarily a first-to-file country. A distributor can apply to register your brand, and getting it back can be expensive. When a distributor has registered a client's mark, we can usually negotiate an assignment if the distributor wants to keep the relationship, and the odds improve when its real money comes from manufacturing the client's products for export. Refusals tend to come from distributors that do not make the products or that earn more using the brand in China themselves.
A Norwegian company once asked us about suing its former Chinese distributor, which was manufacturing and selling the Norwegian company's products in China. The mark had been registered to a Chinese individual who was licensing it to the former distributor. What the company thought was a straightforward breach-of-contract claim had become a much harder case.
Register the mark in your company's own name before the distributor starts using your brand. At the very least, get your application on file first, though a pending application is not the equivalent of an issued registration. Choose your Chinese-language brand name yourself. If you leave that decision entirely to your distributor or the market, Chinese customers can end up knowing your product by a name someone else picked. We give the distributor only the trademark rights it needs to market and sell our client's products. Those rights end with the distribution agreement, subject to any agreed inventory sell-off rights. The distributor may not register the client's marks, Chinese names, logos, domains, or confusingly similar brands. Where a registered mark is licensed, we address recordal of the license with the Chinese trademark authorities. An unrecorded license is generally valid between the parties but cannot be asserted against good-faith third parties. If the distributor will receive valuable confidential information, we consider the protections in our China NNN agreement guide.
Before granting distribution rights, we check whether the product needs testing, certification, registration, Chinese labeling, or import permits. The agreement says who obtains and pays for each approval. If the distributor is responsible, we set a deadline and specify the consequences for missing it. Without that, a foreign supplier can wait indefinitely for sales that cannot legally begin.
I always want to know whose name will appear on each approval. An American medical device company we represented let its Chinese distributor act as its registration agent because the distributor offered to handle the paperwork at no charge. Five years later, the company wanted a stronger distributor. The old one was sitting on the registration certificate and the technical file and had no reason to cooperate. Every month it stalled was a month without sales. Where Chinese rules allow, we usually want the registration in our client's name.
The agreement specifies who handles warranty service and pays for recalls, including whether the supplier warrants directly to end customers or only to the distributor. Those provisions do not automatically shield the manufacturer from Chinese product-liability claims. If the distributor has few assets and inadequate insurance, its promise to indemnify the manufacturer is not worth much after a major product problem.
Chinese distributors often ask for nationwide exclusivity. A distributor that knows the Shanghai market well does not necessarily have useful contacts in Chengdu or Guangzhou, and I rarely like granting rights to all of China without a strong business reason. We define the territory, products, and customers the distributor's rights cover, and whether our client keeps the right to sell directly or appoint other distributors.
We have seen companies sign five-year exclusive agreements and learn, two or three years in, that the distributor never placed a single order. The distributor signed to keep the product off the market while selling its own competing line, a pattern I describe in International Distribution Agreements: Beware the Eager Distributor. During the exclusive period, we generally bar the distributor from handling competing products, after checking that restriction against the competition law that applies.

Our client can appoint another distributor for the uncovered market and keep the Shanghai relationship if it still makes commercial sense.
Clients worried about heavy discounting sometimes want to require their Chinese distributors to maintain minimum resale prices. China's rules effective February 1, 2026 provide only a narrow safe harbor for certain fixed or minimum resale-price restrictions. Where the supplier has multiple distributors, their market shares in the same relevant market and the turnover of the covered goods are aggregated. Even if those thresholds are met, the safe harbor does not apply where evidence shows the agreement eliminates or restricts competition.
For most clients, we focus on the supplier's wholesale price and let the distributor determine its own resale prices. None of our clients has ever had a real resale-price problem in China, but a number of distributors have threatened to sue our clients or report them to the authorities when relationships turned rocky, claiming minimum prices our clients never imposed. When resale price control matters to the business, we review the specific restriction and the law that applies before anyone signs. Form contracts imported from other countries cause enough trouble that we do not rely on whatever price clause the client's standard agreement contains.
I keep seeing the same fight start before a single order is placed. The supplier assumes the distributor will pay for advertising in exchange for exclusivity. Once the distributor establishes a payment history, a client may decide to offer 30-day terms. If it does, the agreement needs a way to return to advance payment when the distributor pays late or its finances deteriorate. We often put prices in a separate schedule, with a defined procedure for updating them, rather than locking prices into a long-term contract.
Shipping terms create avoidable disputes when the parties use familiar acronyms without understanding what they require, so identify the Incoterms rule and the named place. The contract term ought to reflect the product and the investment required. We start some relationships with a trial period and others with a longer term and regular purchase targets.
Unlike the law in some other countries, Chinese law generally does not give ordinary distributors a special statutory right to goodwill compensation simply because a distribution agreement ends. We never make both languages equally authoritative, because that invites an avoidable fight over what the parties agreed to.
When the defendant and its assets are in China, Chinese courts are generally the more direct and less expensive choice. I also think highly of CIETAC arbitration. State-owned enterprises often insist on it, and I prefer it when the distributor is in a smaller city where the local court is a concern. With CIETAC, freezing a distributor's assets still requires a Chinese court. We tend to leave the dispute-resolution provision until late in the drafting, and sometimes have two to five of our lawyers discuss jurisdiction and governing law before settling on it.
An English trading name and an informal signature do not establish which Chinese legal entity agreed to the deal. The agreement needs the distributor's correct registered Chinese legal name, and we normally also require its official company seal, or chop.
If a distributor registers our client's brand, sells outside its agreed territory, or keeps using the trademark after termination, our client needs a contract that clearly prohibits that conduct and provides a remedy that works under Chinese law. We frequently include contract damages provisions for those breaches. Those provisions can help define the monetary claim and support an application for property preservation, including a bank-account freeze. A damages clause does not freeze assets by itself. The court decides whether to grant preservation and can require security. Chinese companies generally understand what a damages clause can lead to in their own courts, which makes it one of the best tools we have for getting them to honor the contract. Pages of broad American-style indemnification language will not cure a contract that lacks usable remedies under Chinese law.
When a distribution relationship ends, the distributor is still holding whatever it has not sold. Without an agreed procedure, the parties fight over whether the distributor can sell the remaining inventory, whether the supplier must buy it back, and at what price. We answer those questions in the agreement, along with pending orders and continuing warranty obligations, while the two sides are still on speaking terms.
The foreign supplier needs some of the distributor's customer information to keep selling in China, even if the distributor built those customer relationships. Where those records contain personal information, China's Personal Information Protection Law governs how they are handled and when they can be sent outside China. The agreement must account for those limits instead of promising an unrestricted transfer. We establish who controls the Chinese websites, e-commerce storefronts, social media accounts, and domain names used to sell the brand. If a product approval cannot legally or practically be transferred, the contract needs realistic cooperation obligations rather than a meaningless promise to hand everything over.

One of our clients owned the molds a Chinese factory was using to manufacture its products. The contract made that ownership clear, but when the client decided to move production, the factory refused to return them. We worked with Chinese litigation counsel to sue and seek an order preserving the factory's assets. The court froze the factory's bank accounts in about five days, and the factory released the molds the next day. I wish more international disputes ended that quickly. Of the thousands of China manufacturing agreements we have drafted, this is the only time a factory has tried to keep a client's molds. The details, including why the contract mattered, are in our article on recovering molds from overseas factories.
I have also spoken with lawyers who won substantial U.S. judgments against foreign businesses before asking us how to collect. Sometimes the defendant had no assets an American court could reach, and collecting overseas meant another expensive proceeding with uncertain prospects. Telling someone that a costly judgment is probably worthless is not a conversation I enjoy. This is the problem behind International Litigation: Winning the Lawsuit Is Often the Easy Part.
Most international disputes we see start with ordinary business problems. A supplier takes a deposit and never ships, or a distributor stops paying while continuing to sell the client's products. Often the contract points to one country while the debtor's assets are in another. The options include negotiation, an emergency asset freeze, a lawsuit at home, a lawsuit where the defendant keeps its money, and arbitration if the parties agreed to it. Sometimes the best advice is not to sue. Before recommending anything, I want to know who owes the obligation, where the assets are, and which forum offers a practical remedy.
Start with the documents, including the ones you would rather your lawyer never see. Save the agreements, amendments, purchase orders, invoices, shipping and inspection records, payment records, and correspondence about the disputed obligations. Preserve communications showing promises your employees made, specifications they changed, payments they missed, or delays they approved. An international litigator who first learns the bad facts from opposing counsel is already behind.

When Negotiation or Mediation Makes Sense

Settlement becomes possible when the other side has a reason to make a deal. A supplier may want future orders. A debtor whose bank accounts have been frozen wants access to its money. Before negotiating, I want to know what the other side needs and what it can deliver. Repeating that our client has a strong case does little when the defendant thinks it can ignore us.

Mediation can work even in very large disputes. Our firm represented the Government of Haiti in a dispute with a Chinese construction company that ended in a private mediation settlement of nearly $35 million after approximately two years. Keep watching limitation periods and other deadlines while negotiations or mediation continue, and do not assume the discussions suspend them.

A settlement needs to be enforceable where performance is expected. Identify the actual obligated entity and any guarantors, address payment security and installments, and specify when claims are released. If a Chinese company is paying money or releasing goods in China, we usually want a Chinese-language agreement that works under Chinese law and before the likely enforcement court. In one cross-border credit dispute we wrote about, incomplete settlement documents helped turn an apparent resolution into further litigation.

Getting Paid After a Judgment or Arbitration Award

A U.S. judgment ordinarily must be recognized under the law of the foreign country before the creditor can use local enforcement procedures. The defendant may raise objections concerning jurisdiction, service, finality, or public policy. Collection is then governed by the law where the assets are located. A creditor cannot simply present an American judgment to a foreign bank and demand payment.

Chinese courts have become more receptive to recognizing certain American judgments under an evolving reciprocity framework. Enforcement is not automatic. Jurisdiction, service, and the judgment's eligibility under current Chinese law all require careful review by Chinese counsel.

Arbitral awards ordinarily follow a different recognition framework, including the New York Convention where applicable. Even after recognition, the creditor needs assets it can lawfully reach. I reassess the economics before filing and whenever the next stage, including enforcement, requires substantial expense.

When a Foreign Supplier Dispute Involves Fraud

In a Yiwu supplier fraud matter, a buyer paid about $177,000 to a Chinese intermediary for three shipments. The first, worth approximately $35,000, arrived. The other goods never left China. According to the buyer, the intermediary passed only a small portion of the payment to the manufacturer, then spent months claiming that goods were nearly finished or had shipped. The buyer even sent representatives to investigate, but the promised deliveries never materialized.

We recommended that the buyer retain a reputable Chinese lawyer experienced in economic-crime complaints to evaluate a police referral. The alleged failure to fund production, coupled with false shipment claims, warranted examining whether the conduct was intentional fraud. We could not promise the police would accept the case, because Chinese authorities can treat a failed commercial transaction as a civil dispute.

Do not threaten criminal prosecution to collect an ordinary commercial debt. That can create legal problems of its own. When the evidence genuinely suggests fraud, counsel should evaluate criminal reporting alongside the civil claims and deadlines. Banks, payment platforms, insurers, and marketplaces may also offer recovery options worth investigating before financing an international lawsuit.

Defending Against Foreign Lawsuits and Judgments

Companies sometimes disregard a foreign court summons because they have no operations in the country, believe the plaintiff is bluffing, or think a judgment issued there cannot affect them. An arbitration notice can be dismissed just as casually. That is a serious gamble. A foreign court may proceed to a default judgment, and an arbitral tribunal can issue an award when a properly notified respondent refuses to participate. The plaintiff may later attempt enforcement wherever the defendant has assets.

When foreign legal papers arrive, preserve the record and have counsel calculate the response deadline immediately. The first review should cover jurisdiction, service or arbitral notice, contractual forum requirements, and whether an appearance or objection affects available defenses. Check insurance and indemnification rights, related proceedings, and possible counterclaims. An ill-considered response can waive defenses that would otherwise remain available.

We also defend companies and owners when foreign creditors seek recognition of judgments in the United States. Recognition of foreign-country money judgments here is primarily governed by state law, often through a version of the Uniform Foreign-Country Money Judgments Recognition Act. The creditor ordinarily has to establish that the judgment qualifies for recognition, and the debtor can raise permitted defenses, including jurisdictional or serious notice and due-process defects. A U.S. court does not normally reopen the foreign case just because the debtor thinks the foreign judge got the facts wrong.

These cases often turn on old records: who was served, whether the defendant appeared, whether it objected to jurisdiction, and what happened in the foreign proceeding. The defense must fit the recognition law of the U.S. state where the creditor filed. The Questions I Ask Before Hiring Foreign Litigation Counsel

Some years ago, I came across an email from one of our international litigators to a client considering a lawsuit in a small emerging-market country. The client wanted to know whether the claim was worth pursuing and which local firm to hire. Our lawyer had listed the questions we planned to ask the firms under consideration. I still use much the same list today.

  1. Which court has jurisdiction, and does a forum clause or arbitration agreement change that? Could another country also hear the dispute?
  2. Would a judge, jury, or panel decide the case, and how experienced are they with disputes involving foreign companies?
  3. What evidence will the court accept, what authentication or translation is required, and how much weight does it give live testimony?
  4. Can we compel documents or testimony from the defendant or third parties? Are pretrial depositions or other discovery procedures available?
  5. Can the court resolve weak claims or defenses before a full trial?
  6. Is corruption a credible concern in this court? Does the opposing party have political or economic influence, and are foreign litigants treated fairly?
  7. Can we freeze assets, obtain an injunction, preserve evidence, or secure goods? What proof or security is required?
  8. What will each stage cost, including court fees, lawyers, experts, translation, travel, security, appeals, and enforcement? Give us a realistic range, not an optimistic estimate.
  9. Can the winner recover legal fees or costs? Which expenses qualify, and are contingency or alternative fee arrangements permitted?
  10. How long do emergency relief, the first decision, appeals, and collection typically take? What causes delays?
  11. When do comparable cases settle, and what usually brings the defendant to the table?
  12. What defenses, counterclaims, or weaknesses in our documents and conduct concern you most? What have we overlooked?
  13. Where are the defendant's assets, how can we investigate them before filing, and how effective is collection in this jurisdiction?
  14. Who will actually handle the case? How much of the firm's practice is litigation, how often does it represent foreign clients, and what happened in comparable cases?
  15. What would make you advise us not to sue? What is the worst likely outcome, what are the realistic collection prospects, and is the case worth the money?

That last question matters most to me. I distrust lawyers who assure an unfamiliar foreign client that it has an excellent case before examining the contract, the other side's likely evidence, and the defendant's assets. If the proposed local counsel cannot explain what might defeat the claim or make it uneconomic, I keep looking.

Frequently Asked Questions About International Commercial Disputes

Can my company sue a foreign company in the United States?

Yes, if the court has subject-matter jurisdiction, venue is proper, and there is a valid basis for personal jurisdiction over the defendant. The defendant's U.S. contacts or agreement to litigate here often matter. American assets can help with collection but do not, by themselves, establish personal jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. If the assets are overseas, enforcement ordinarily requires a separate recognition proceeding.

Is international arbitration better than suing in court?

Neither is better across the board. Arbitration offers an enforcement advantage when the debtor has assets in several countries because of the New York Convention. It also brings institutional and arbitrator fees and limited opportunities to challenge an award. When a Chinese manufacturer and its assets are in China, we often prefer litigation in the right Chinese court.

How long does an international commercial dispute take?

An emergency asset freeze can come within days in some courts, as it did in our mold case. A decision on the merits, an appeal, and actual collection take longer, particularly when enforcement requires proceedings in another country. Ask foreign counsel for separate estimates for each stage.

What size dispute is worth pursuing?

Our usual screening threshold for straightforward litigation or arbitration in China is about $350,000. Below that, we generally advise against routine money claims because legal costs consume too much of the likely recovery. Chinese law sets no such minimum. Smaller claims involving essential tooling or injunctive relief can justify litigation, while much larger claims against defendants with no reachable assets may not.

What if a government-owned foreign company owes us money?

State ownership does not necessarily confer sovereign immunity. Depending on the entity and claim, immunity statutes or treaties may apply. Immunity from suit and immunity from enforcement are separate questions, and a waiver permitting litigation does not necessarily authorize attachment of government property. Before filing, determine the entity's legal status, the nature of the transaction, and which assets can lawfully be reached.

Can lawsuits or arbitrations proceed in more than one country?

Yes, particularly when multiple companies are involved or contracts contain inconsistent dispute resolution provisions. Parallel proceedings increase expense and the risk of conflicting orders. Rules concerning stays, parallel proceedings, and the effect of earlier decisions vary by jurisdiction. We coordinate filings with local counsel so that a move in one country does not undermine the case elsewhere.

What if our evidence or contract is in another language?

The governing language clause and the original contract text matter. A Chinese court will not necessarily rely on an English summary, and other courts may require sworn translations or specific authentication procedures. Translation can add material cost in an arbitration or a document-heavy case, and poor translations can change the apparent meaning of contractual obligations. Preserve the originals and have lawyers who understand the relevant language review key provisions before filing.

Can we recover legal fees if we win?

Fee recovery depends on the governing law, the contract, and the forum. American litigation normally follows the American rule, subject to statutory, contractual, and other exceptions. Some foreign courts award specified costs, and arbitral tribunals may allocate costs under the agreement and applicable rules. Even an award of legal fees must be collected. Budget on the assumption that you will have to pay your own lawyers.
